# 📊 What is Data Science? {.subsection background-color="#425556"}


## A **_Practical_** definition {background-image="images/chrome-capture-2026-10-15.png" background-size="300px" background-position="90% 10%" background-opacity="0.5"} 

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}

This is the first question you may have in mind when approaching the topic of Data Science. We think that a first answer to this question comes from a practical standpoint, i.e. from what Data Science _does_.  To cite a [post by Ally Heinrich on the Harvard Business School blog](https://online.hbs.edu/blog/post/data-analytics-vs-data-science) (emphasis ours): 

![](images/chrome-capture-2026-10-15.png){fig-alt="A screenshot of the HBS blog post title" fig-align="center" width="90%"}

> Data science centers on **collecting, preparing, modeling, and analyzing data** to build predictive capabilities and solve complex problems.
> 
> As [HBS Professor Karim] Lakhani notes in Data Science and AI for Decision Making, data science “focuses on **transforming raw data** into **practical understanding** that **informs decisions**."
>
> To achieve this, data scientists leverage a combination of technical tools and methodologies [...] 

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

A _practical_ definition[^1]: what Data Science **_does_**:

. . . 

>  [...] data science centers on **collecting, preparing, modeling, and analyzing data** to build predictive capabilities and solve complex problems.

. . .

> [...] data science “focuses on **transforming raw data** into **practical understanding** that informs decisions."

. . .

> To achieve this, data scientists leverage a **combination of technical tools and methodologies** [...]


[^1]: Heinrich, Ally. “What’s the Difference between Data Analytics & Data Science?” Harvard Business School, 18 June 2026, [online.hbs.edu/blog/post/data-analytics-vs-data-science](online.hbs.edu/blog/post/data-analytics-vs-data-science). Accessed 15 Oct. 2026. 

:::

# What is R? {.subsection background-color="#425556"}

## A brief overview

:::{.fragment}
::: {.content-box-oil}
**R** is an open source **programming language** designed for **statistical computing**
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
::: {.content-box-oil}
**R** is **highly extensible through `{packages}`** that can be **developed by anyone**.
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
::: {.content-box-oil}
**Packages** are **collections of functions** that expand the functionality of R.
:::
:::

## **R** as your **workbench** {background-image="images/elmer-canas-1UimDTf69ho-unsplash.jpg"background-position="cover" background-opacity="0.3"}

:::{.fragment}
::: {.content-box-oil}
**Data**: the **materials** you're working with (metal, or wood)
:::
:::

. . . 

:::{.fragment}
::: {.content-box-oil}
**Functions**: the **tools** you use to transform the materials (saw, hammers, pliers)
:::
:::

. . .

:::{.fragment}
::: {.content-box-oil}
**Packages**: the **toolboxes** that contain a bunch of useful tools.
:::
:::

## `{tidyverse}`: Another flavour of R. {background-image="images/tidyverse-logo.png" background-size="150px" background-position="90% 90%"}


Base **R** is **powerful** but a bit **hard to learn**

::: {.content-box-marine}
One of the main problems: **many different ways to organise data**.
:::

::: {.notes}
- functions have same names, they don't communicate well with each other
- the output of one does not become easily the input of another (especially if they come from different packages)
- `lists` are the preferred data source
- "Freedom comes at a price" lists are powerful but can lead to those inconsistencies
:::

## {.center}

![](images/tidydata_2-1-mod.png){fig-alt="Cartoon showing that tidy datasets all look alike and can be combined easily, while every messy dataset is messy in its own way." fig-align="center" width="80%"}

:::
:::




## `{tidyverse}`: Another flavour of R. {background-image="images/tidyverse-logo.png" background-size="150px" background-position="90% 90%"}


Enter the **`{tidyverse}`**, "an *opinionated* collection of packages"

::: {.content-box-marine}
The Data is **organised in single, consistent way**: **"tidy" data**.
:::

::: {.notes}
-   "opinionated" they are directive, i.e. they come with a set of rules and guidelines
:::

### ▶️️ The Pipe operator

## 🗄️ Datasets in variables

To work with data in R, **assign the dataset** to a **variable**

```{r eval=FALSE}
rolling_stones_data <- read_csv("data/rolling_stones.csv")
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
rolling_stones_data <- readr::read_csv("data/rolling_stones.csv")

dplyr::slice_head(rolling_stones_data)
```

. . .

You can **use more than one dataset** in your session, by **storing them in different variables**

```{r eval=FALSE}
# reading a dataset: rolling_stones
rolling_stones_data <- read_csv("data/rolling_stones.csv")

# reading another dataset: sales
sales_data <- read_tsv("data/sales_data.tsv", skip = 3)
```

::: {.notes}
Here, talk about data types:

-   `slice_head()` gives you the first row of a dataset
-   you see here the `chr`, `numeric` etc.? : It means that every column has a *type*
:::

## 🗄️ Data Formats

::: {.content-box-marine}
In this workshop, we will focus on **data that comes in tables**, like **MS Excel**.
:::

. . .

But, in R you can work with **many different data structures**, such as:

-   **structured** databases, like an **SQL** database

-   **unstructured** databases, such as **json** and **xml** files

-   **raw text** and **html code**

-   even **STATA, SAS and SPSS data**!

. . .

::: {.content-box-marine}
We are not limited by a particular data format when using **R**
:::

## 🧰 Packages {background-image="images/dplyr-logo.png" background-size="200px" background-position="90% 90%"}

::: {.content-box-marine}
We said that **R** is highly extensible through *packages*.
:::

-   In a project we only use the tools we need.

-   Thus, we **only attach** the packages **we need**.

(After all, nobody likes a messy workbench!)

::: {.notes}
-   Mention Excel, photoshop, browser *plugins*
-   "There's a package for that"
:::

## 🧰 Installing and Attaching R Packages {.smaller}

To **use** the functions in a package, we need to do **two things**:

:::::: {.columns}
::::: {.column width="50%"}

:::: {.content-box-oil}
[1. **Install** the package]{.box-title}

::: {.content-box-white}
[We only have to do this **once**.]{.box-body}

[⚠️ **Do not include this** in your **source code!**]{.box-body}

``` r
# install the package dplyr
install.packages("dplyr")
```
:::
::::

:::::

::::: {.column width="50%"}

:::: {.content-box-oil}
[2. **Attach** the package]{.box-title}

::: {.content-box-white}
[This you need to do in **each session**.]{.box-body}

[⚠️ **Include this** in your **source code!**]{.box-body}

``` r
# attach the package dplyr
library(dplyr)
```
:::
::::

:::::
::::::

## 🧰 Example: using `dplyr::slice_head()`

-   The function `slice_head()` allows us to view **the first line(s)** of a dataset.

-   This function `slice_head()` is part of the Package `{dplyr}`.

-   Let's use it on the `cars` dataset.

. . .

```{r}
# attaching the package
library(dplyr)

# using the function slice_head() on the dataset cars
slice_head(cars)
```

**Success!!**

## ⁉ Asking for help

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
If you want to know what a function does, all you need to do is type:

1.  a question mark `?`

2.  the name of the function you want to know more about

For instance:

``` r
?slice_head()
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/help.png){fig-alt="The RStudio Help pane showing the documentation page for a function, with its description, usage and arguments." fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

## ▶️ The *Pipe* operator of the `{tidyverse}`

::: {.content-box-marine}
Allows us to **write code *sequentially*** which makes it **easy to read and write** complex calls.
:::

. . .

**Example:** Plotting the density of the variable `speed` in the `cars` dataset

``` r
# nested
plot(density(cars$speed))

# with the pipe
cars %>% pull(speed) %>% density() %>% plot()
```

. . .

Which can be "read" as:

> "*take the dataset `cars` **then** `pull()` the variable `speed` **then** compute the `density()`**then** build a `plot()`.*"


## ▶️ The *Pipe* operator of the `{tidyverse}`

::: {.content-box-marine}
The *pipe* `%>%` **"feeds" the left-hand side** as the **first argument** of the next function.
:::

Use the shortcut: <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>M</kbd> (<kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>M</kbd> on a Mac)

## ▶️ `%>%` or `|>`?

Since version 4.1, R also has a **native pipe** `|>`, built into the language.

``` r
cars %>% pull(speed) %>% density() %>% plot() # the {tidyverse} pipe
cars |> pull(speed) |> density() |> plot()    # the native pipe
```

-   For everyday use, they **do the same thing**, and you will meet both in code online.
-   In this workshop, we use `%>%`.

::: callout-tip
## Which pipe does the shortcut insert?

In RStudio, go to *Tools* → *Global Options* → *Code* and look for *Use native pipe operator, \|\> (requires R 4.1+)*. Unticked, the shortcut inserts `%>%`; ticked, it inserts `|>`. The workshop project is set to `%>%`.
:::

# 💾 Extra info: Saving today's work {.subsection background-color="#425556"}

## 💾 Saving one file

::: {.content-box-marine}
Your Renku session is **temporary**: before it ends, **download** the files you want to keep to your computer.
:::

Most of your work is in **one file**: the exercise notebook.

-   In the **Files** pane, go to `workshop-content/_exercises/`.

-   **Tick the box** next to `exercise-notebook.qmd`.

-   Click on **More** ⚙️ → **Export...** → **Download**.

. . .

::: callout-tip
Tick **one file at a time**. Exporting a whole folder fails on Renku. 
:::

## 💾 Saving all scripts at once

- To download **all your notebooks and scripts** (`.qmd`, `.Rmd` and `.R`) at once, first pack them into a single archive. 

. . .

- Type in the **Console**:

```{r}
#| eval: false
tar("my-work.tar.gz",
    files = list.files("workshop-content",
                       pattern = "[.](qmd|Rmd|R)$",
                       recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE),
    compression = "gzip", tar = "internal")
```

- Then download `my-work.tar.gz` as on the previous slide.

- On your computer, **double-click** it to unpack it (macOS and Windows 11).

. . . 

::: callout-important
Rendered pages and their support files can be recreated by rendering again.
:::
